What moves the price on a 4N14 is the power tune (150 hp vs 177 hp), the condition of the balance shaft coupling (a known wear item), the state of the piezo injectors, and whether the DPF and EGR system have been properly maintained. A reconditioned unit that includes a new balance shaft coupling, refurbished injectors, and a cleaned DPF commands a premium over a used take‑out. See our full reconditioned engine cost guide.

failures.title: Mitsubishi 4N14 Engine Problems - What Actually Fails

items.title: Balance Shaft Coupling Wear - The 4N14's Most Notorious Issue
items.whatHappens: The 4N14 has a known, widespread issue with balance shaft coupling wear. The genuine coupling is made of soft material and wears out relatively quickly. When it fails, it produces a loud ticking or rattling noise at idle - described by some owners as sounding like "a bag of spanners left inside the engine". If left unaddressed, the drive gear teeth can fail, leading to catastrophic engine failure of surrounding housing and bearings. This issue affects all 4N14 engines regardless of year.
items.repairVsReplace: Balance shaft coupling replacement is a specialist job (£500-£1,200) and should be done as soon as the ticking noise appears. Aftermarket heat‑treated couplings are available that offer better durability than genuine parts. If the coupling has failed completely and damaged surrounding components, a full engine replacement may be required. Read our full balance shaft failure guide

items.title: Piezo Injector Failure - Poor Fuel Quality Sensitivity
items.whatHappens: The 4N14 uses high‑tech piezo injectors that are extremely sensitive to fuel quality. Low‑quality fuel or fuel contamination can cause injector failure, leading to misfires, rough idling, reduced fuel efficiency, and poor starting. Injector replacement is an expensive procedure.
items.repairVsReplace: Injector cleaning may help in early stages, but failure typically requires replacement (£300-£500 per injector). Replacement of all four injectors is often recommended if one has failed. This does not typically require engine replacement. Read our full injector failure guide

items.title: DPF & EGR System Issues - Urban Driving & Regeneration Problems
items.whatHappens: The 4N14's DPF and EGR system is prone to clogging, particularly on vehicles used primarily for short urban journeys where the DPF cannot complete a regeneration cycle. During DPF regeneration, a certain amount of diesel fuel enters the engine oil, causing oil dilution. This can lead to increased oil levels, reduced oil effectiveness, and in severe cases, engine damage. The EGR valve also clogs up quickly, and intake flaps can stick from soot buildup.
items.repairVsReplace: DPF cleaning is a specialist job (£200-£600). EGR valve cleaning or replacement is also manageable (£200-£500). These are repairable issues and rarely require engine replacement. Read our full DPF failure guide

items.title: Timing Chain & Tensioner Wear - Rattling & Performance Loss
items.whatHappens: The 4N14 uses a timing chain that can stretch over time, particularly on engines with extended oil change intervals. The tensioner is prone to failure, which can be heard as a rattling/ticking sound from the left corner of the valve cover. If the chain skips, it can cause pistons to contact valves, resulting in catastrophic engine failure.
items.repairVsReplace: If caught early (rattling only), timing chain and tensioner replacement is a manageable repair (£800-£1,500). If the chain has jumped and valves have contacted pistons, the engine is typically beyond economical repair - a full replacement is the only option.

failures.goodYearsLine: The 4N14 has been produced since 2010, with continuous updates. However, the balance shaft coupling issue affects all years. Post‑2016 engines benefit from improved DPF regeneration strategies, but the fundamental design vulnerabilities remain. Regular servicing (oil changes every 5,000-8,000 miles with 5W‑30 oil) and using high‑quality fuel are essential to minimise injector and DPF issues. Valve clearance adjustment is required every 45,000 km (28,000 miles).

variants.title: How to Confirm You Have the 4N14
variants.intro: The 4N14 is Mitsubishi's 2.2‑litre DI‑D diesel engine, part of the 4N1 family which also includes the 1.8L 4N13 and 2.4L 4N15. It is an all‑aluminium engine with a chain‑driven timing system, MIVEC variable valve timing, and common‑rail direct injection. Where the code appears: - Stamped on a metal plate on the engine block (left‑hand side) - On the V5C logbook under "Engine number" (the first 4 characters will read 4N14) - Via Mitsubishi VIN decoder Commonly confused with: - 4N13 - 1.8‑litre DI‑D (150 hp), smaller displacement, different bore/stroke - 4N15 - 2.4‑litre DI‑D, larger capacity, used in later L200 and Triton - [4D56 - LINK PENDING - page not in current inventory] - older 2.5‑litre diesel, completely different engine architecture

relatives.description: LINK PENDING - page not in current inventory] - the older 2.5‑litre diesel engine used in earlier Mitsubishi models. Used different injection technology (indirect injection or earlier common‑rail) and was less refined - the 4N14 introduced modern common‑rail and MIVEC technology for improved efficiency and power.

- the 2.4‑litre DI‑D diesel engine introduced in the later L200 and Triton models. Larger displacement and more torque - the 4N15 is not a straight swap with the 4N14 due to different ECU calibration and ancillaries.

buyingGuide.title: Buying a Replacement 4N14 - What to Choose

options.label: Used
options.body: ** A used 4N14 can make sense for lower‑value Outlander or ASX models where the car's value doesn't justify a recon unit. However, the balance shaft coupling, injectors and DPF are the biggest risks - only consider a used unit with documented proof of recent balance shaft coupling replacement, injector service, and DPF cleaning. Without that, factor in £1,000-£2,000 for preventative work (coupling, injectors, DPF). Link once: /services/used-engines

options.label: Reconditioned
options.body: ** A proper 4N14 recon is the best option for owners planning to keep their car long‑term, especially for the heavier Outlander and Delica where the engine works harder. A quality recon should include: full strip and inspection, new balance shaft coupling (critical, with upgraded aftermarket part if possible), new injectors or full refurbishment, DPF and EGR cleaning, new timing chain and tensioner, valve clearance adjustment, new gaskets and seals, and a full test. With a 12-24 month warranty, this gives you peace of mind that the engine's known weaknesses have been addressed - well worth the £1,800-£2,800 supply cost. Link once: /services/reconditioned-engines

options.label: Rebuilt
options.body: ** A full rebuild is justified when the original engine has suffered catastrophic failure (balance shaft coupling failure causing housing damage, chain jump with valve damage, severe DPF blockage leading to oil dilution and bearing failure) and the car is a cherished keeper or low‑mileage example. An upgraded rebuild should include new pistons/rings, refreshed cylinder head, new balance shaft coupling, new timing chain and guides, and a full DPF/turbo overhaul. This is specialist territory and typically only makes sense for cars with strong residual value. Link once: /services/rebuilt-engines

buyingGuide.supplyFitLine: ** All engines can be supplied and fitted through our network of vetted Mitsubishi diesel specialists nationwide, with 12‑month warranty on reconditioned and rebuilt units. Link once: /services/supply-and-fit
buyingGuide.vehicleValueNote: ** The 4N14 sits in Mitsubishi Outlander, ASX, Lancer, Delica and Eclipse Cross - cars now worth £3,000-£18,000 depending on age and condition. With a reconditioned supply cost of £1,800-£2,800, replacement is viable on most examples. However, for a sub‑£3,000 Outlander or ASX with high mileage and a failed engine, a used unit (£800-£1,500) with documented history may be the only sensible option. For cars worth under £2,000, consider breaking the car before committing to a replacement engine. For the heavier Outlander and Delica where the 4N14 works harder, a reconditioned unit is strongly recommended to ensure longevity and reliability.

items.question: How do I confirm if my car has the 4N14 or the 4N13?
items.answer: Check the engine code stamped on the block (left-hand side) - it will read 4N14 for the 2.2‑litre variant, or 4N13 for the 1.8‑litre variant. The V5C logbook also lists the full engine number, with the first 4 characters identifying the code. 4N14: 2.2L DI‑D, 150-177 hp, used in Outlander, ASX, Lancer. 4N13: 1.8L DI‑D, 150 hp, used in ASX and Lancer (some markets). Fitting the wrong variant is not a straight swap - different bore/stroke, ECU and ancillaries.

items.question: How long does a 4N14 engine typically last?
items.answer: With meticulous maintenance and early preventative work, these engines can exceed 150,000-200,000 miles. The 4N14 is fundamentally a robust engine; the limiting factors are the balance shaft coupling, injectors and DPF system. Balance shaft coupling replacement recommended at 60k-80k miles as preventative. Injectors: use quality fuel and regular servicing (5,000-8,000 miles with 5W‑30 oil). Valve clearance adjustment required every 45,000 km (28,000 miles).
